chapter_theme: Civakan hears the Jain teacher's sermon: all embodied life is suffering, even the gods' pleasures end in the fading garland and the grief of their fall, and release from birth is what even they beg for; he is told of the Lord's marks, karma that spares no rank, and the discipline of sila, ending with the fruit of giving.

cast.role: the hero, now hearing the Jain teacher's sermon
the Jain teacher who instructs Civakan on suffering, the gods, sila and giving (not named in these verses)
the gods of the heavens whose pleasures and fall the teacher describes
the goddesses and consorts of the gods

2799.reading: The Jain teacher opens by telling the hero that for men everything is suffering: wishes unmet, parting from those one longs for, bright youth leaving and old age arriving, and being scorned for lack of learning.
2799.nuance: The unit closes with என்றான், so the poet reports the teacher's words; the teacher is not named in these verses and is identified only from the sermon's address to Civakan (வேலோய், 2799; வேந்தே, 2807; வேந்தர் வேந்தே, 2810).
2799.event: The teacher begins his sermon to Civakan with the suffering of the human state.

claims.claim: human life is suffering: wants unfulfilled, parting from the loved, loss of youth, old age, contempt

2800.reading: The teacher begins on the gods: they are not born in a womb, do not touch the ground, their forms cannot be painted, and their bodies shine like the sun while their garlands never fade.
2800.nuance: A description of celestial bodies given as the first step of an argument that even such lives are suffering (2810-2811).

claims.claim: gods arise without a womb and do not touch the earth

2801.reading: The gods' women are pictured limb by limb: palms and feet like lotuses, red eyes, coral mouths, bright teeth, and a glance that gathers fierce force.
2801.nuance: Line 4 (வெங்கடை மழைக்கண் நோக்கி வெய்துறத் திரண்ட) is hard, and the last clause is read only roughly.

2802.reading: The gods wear jewelled garlands, diamond bows and glowing ear-rings, and when they long for the nectar that is their food they take it by mind alone.

claims.claim: gods take their food by mere wish of the mind

2803.reading: The goddesses with long eyes and bows for brows, their girdles gleaming, fall into the flower bed bewildered by the arrows of the god of love.
2803.event: Celestial women, struck by Kama's arrows, fall into the flower bed.

2804.reading: Gods clasp the flower-branch women to their full and, though lust churns the heart like a sea, will not let them go, as if these women were the raft for crossing it.
2804.nuance: The raft image turns on irony: the sea is lust and the raft is the thing that keeps them in it. The reading of நீத்துநீர் is not secure.
2804.event: The gods embrace their women and do not release them.

claims.claim: the gods cling to the objects of lust as though to a raft across the sea of lust and cannot let go

2805.reading: As the women's breasts press and tear the garlands, the gods drink them like a roaring sea of nectar and are never sated, nor do they blink.
2805.event: The gods lie with their women and drink them without being satisfied.

2806.reading: As the dancing goddesses jingle girdles and anklets under the wish-trees to the sound of instruments, the gods watch and take their fill of fortune without feeling it enough.
2806.nuance: மானார் is read as 'do not diminish/are not satisfied'; the verse does not say outright that their pleasure fails to satisfy, but the sequence 2805-2810 points that way.
2806.event: The gods watch the goddesses dance.

2807.reading: The teacher tells the king that the gods, cool and weary of nothing, pass their days playing with great elephants whose tusks gore the clouds, their gold ear-rings and ear-ornaments flashing.
2807.nuance: The close (தொழுதகத் கழிப்பர்) looks corrupt; the sense of spending time in play is kept and nothing is built on the last words.
2807.event: The gods pass the days in sport with celestial elephants.

2808.reading: Surrounded by their bangled consorts in the grove of wish-trees, the beings of heaven worship the Lord's feet with folded hands and flowers and beg that release be completed and birth not wanted.
2808.nuance: Line 2 (வாம னடிகையிற் றொழுது) can be read as worship of a named Vamana, of the Lord generally, or of a graceful dancer; the teaching sense, that gods beg release, holds either way.
2808.event: The gods and their women worship the Lord and ask for release.

claims.claim: even the gods ask for release from birth, not for more heaven

2809.reading: After the gods have embraced their women, the next day their radiance fails like the sun that has lost its rays, and they grieve in the heavens.
2809.nuance: Lines 3-4 are damaged (பொற்புகுத் திருப்ப); the grief-at-fading reading is certain only in outline.
2809.event: The gods' splendour fails as their end approaches.

claims.claim: a god's radiance fails as his heavenly life runs out

2810.reading: The teacher tells the king that when fifteen days remain, the gods' eyes begin to blink and their garlands wither, and they grieve, like those who ate poisoned nectar, that the long days of pleasure were worthless.
2810.nuance: The pleasure the verses 2800-2809 described is turned inside out: the same heavenly life is recounted as poison in nectar.
2810.event: The gods see the signs of their approaching fall and regret their pleasure.

claims.claim: fifteen days before a god falls his eyes blink and his garland fades, and he sees his pleasure as wasted

2811.reading: The teacher concludes that even gods are struck down by other gods and made to bow, hear and serve; being born into disease is suffering, and all is suffering for those who have taken a body.
2811.nuance: Line 2 (மணிகமாப் பணிகள்) is garbled; the reading of service under higher gods rests on the other lines.
2811.event: The teacher draws the lesson of the gods' lives: embodiment is suffering.

claims.claim: all embodied existence, even a god's, is suffering
gods suffer subjection to other gods

2812.reading: The Lord who sits on the lion throne under the cool young asoka, worshipped by the gods and dispelling the darkness of every world, is praised, with a wish that his lotus feet rest on the speaker's head.
2812.nuance: The first person (என்றலை) is the teacher's, taken from the sermon's flow; the verse does not name who prays.
2812.event: The teacher praises the Jina enthroned beneath the asoka.

claims.claim: the Jina enthroned under the asoka and worshipped by the gods removes the darkness from all worlds

2813.reading: The one who has three golden walls, three pearl umbrellas, the homage of three worlds, three weapons, three wonders and three dear books, and a sea of sweet virtues, is said to be our lord.
2813.nuance: The threes are listed without names; the identification of the walls, umbrellas and books with Jain tradition is a reading, and படை மூன்றும், நூல் மூன்று are not settled here.

claims.claim: the Jina marked by the threefold signs is the lord to follow

2814.reading: The virtuous, praising the feet of the king of the wheel of dharma who walked on the open lotus, say that the things to be understood are five, six and nine.
2814.nuance: The verse gives the numbers only; that they stand for the Jain groupings of five extended things, six substances and nine principles is a reading from the tradition rather than from the verse.
2814.event: The teacher reports what the righteous hold about the categories of reality.

claims.claim: the objects of knowledge fall into groups of five, six and nine

2815.reading: Knowing that mighty Indra and a small monkey alike eat the fruit of their own deeds, one neither rejoices at the great nor despises the lowly; those who have understood the two kinds of deeds have understood the Lord's scripture.
2815.nuance: Karma is equalizing here: rank in heaven or earth shields no one. The verse says understanding both deeds and the Lord's text go together, so right knowledge is the way, not praise or grace.

claims.claim: every being, from Indra to a monkey, eats the fruit of its own deeds
one who knows this is neither elated by the great nor scornful of the humble

2816.reading: The marks of the one who follows the Lord's dharma are honouring the worthy, freedom from disgust, steady joy, holding the learned in honour, upholding the fallen, teaching dharma, avoiding the mean, letting anger go and curbing pride.
2816.nuance: This looks like a list of the marks of right faith, but the verse's items do not map one for one onto the stock list of eight, so none is asserted here.

claims.claim: the follower of the Jina's dharma honours the worthy, avoids the mean, gives up anger and pride, and is kind to all

2817.reading: Those who have understood what was said briefly are not reborn as beasts or women, do not enter the seven hells, and do not mix with the lowest gods; the speaker adds that he spoke without full knowledge and that some who escape hell may still become beasts in the lands of enjoyment.
2817.nuance: That female birth is ranked as a fall is the sermon's view; the claim is reported, not argued. Line 3 (அறியாது உரைத்தேன் அது நிற்க) is read as the teacher's modest restriction, and its sense is not secure.

claims.claim: those of right understanding are not reborn as animals or women, nor in the seven hells nor among the lowest gods
some who avoid hell are still born as animals in the lands of enjoyment

2818.reading: Sila, the discipline of conduct, is said to be like strung gems: a hundred crore virtues guarded by eighteen thousand guards and divided out by the learned.
2818.nuance: The number eighteen thousand matches a Jain tradition of counting the divisions of sila; the verse gives only the number.

claims.claim: sila is a body of 18,000 guarding rules and a hundred crore virtues

2819.reading: Sila is said to be like the golden armour of warring kings: it withers the intoxication of the five senses and wears away the deeds one does each day.
2819.nuance: செய்வினை நுணுக்குவ is read as thinning karma, not as making one's works finer.

claims.claim: sila blunts the intoxication of the senses and thins one's deeds

2820.reading: The teacher addresses the crowned king and speaks of ascetics who, as bidden, pluck out their gem-like hair with their own hands, bearing it with a patience as heavy as earth and sea.
2820.nuance: The details of lines 3-4 (துணித்தொரு துணிசுமந்தனைய) are obscure and the sense of earth-heavy patience is the safest reading.
2820.event: Ascetics pluck out their hair as a discipline.

claims.claim: plucking out the hair is borne with patience as an austerity

2821.reading: Men who wrong others' wives, who add the goad of slander, and who take into their mouth what another has spat out, do hard things, are they, the verse asks, men born on earth?
2821.nuance: The verse's irony (are they men?) and the unfamiliar spat-out betel make the force uncertain.

claims.claim: adultery and slander and taking another's spat-out leavings are wrongs unworthy of a man

2822.reading: Sila is not conduct alone: those who destroy their inner knowledge by eating honey full of worms and feeding on the wounds of other creatures lose a great gain and are called mere beasts by the great; giving up what they condemn is sila, the teacher said.
2822.nuance: பிறவற்றின் புண் ('the wound of other things') is read as flesh, which the Kural also calls another creature's wound; the verse does not use the word புலால்.

claims.claim: sila is to give up what the great condemn, including honey with worms and flesh
those who destroy inner discernment through such food are beasts

2823.reading: The poet reports that the teacher also explained the gift: seed in good soil grows pleasantly and yields wealth to enrich the field, while seed in barren soil gives thin crops and passes like lightning.
2823.nuance: Here the poet reports what the teacher expounded (விரித்து), so the voice shifts from the teacher's address to narration.
2823.event: The teacher expounds the nature and fruit of giving.

claims.claim: a gift to a worthy recipient grows into great wealth; a gift to the unworthy yields little and vanishes

links.note: Vijayai urged her son, before bright youth lapses and black hair greys, to do hard penance and give; the teacher now lists the lapse of youth and the coming of old age as one of the standing sufferings of men.
links.teaches: The mother's household warning about youth is shown here as one item in a Jain account of suffering, so her urging reads as the doctrine put plainly for a son who might delay.

links.note: The epic lists unmet wishes, parting, lost youth and old age as suffering; the quatrain lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as things that do not last and the best therefore renounce at once.
links.teaches: The epic names the pain of loss where the quatrain names its passing, and the quatrain supplies the action, renouncing without delay, that the epic verse leaves unsaid.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Naladiyar's practical conclusion, to renounce at once, which it does not draw itself
gains.b: The quatrain gains the Jain account of why passing things hurt: wishes unmet and the loved parted from, not mere decay

links.note: The gods watch the goddesses dance and still take their fill of fortune without being content; the opening of the ilampakam says the hero has lost his wish for women whose beauty makes the heavens bow.
links.teaches: The sermon's heavenly pleasures supply the reason for the hero's turn from women in the opening: even the gods' unlimited enjoyment does not satisfy.

links.note: The epic gods, with fifteen days left, blink and see their garlands fade and grieve like those who ate poisoned nectar; the Saiva verse says countless gods have died while the one with the forehead eye stays.
links.teaches: The two texts share the mortality of gods but part on the cure: the Jain verse leaves no god to rest on and moves the hearer to release, the Saiva verse moves him to the one undying Lord.

gains.a: The epic gains a rival answer to the fall of the gods: an unchanging Lord to rest on, which a Jain account of gods without such a Lord lacks
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a concrete picture of how a dying god feels, the signs, the regret at wasted pleasure, that it only states in a line

links.note: The poet announced early that the hero hears the dharma and, afraid of kingship like a snake struck by thunder, renounces; the sermon's lesson that all embodied life, even a god's, is suffering is the content of that dharma.
links.teaches: This unit is the first body of the doctrine whose effect on the hero the early verse reports in a line, so it shows what the renunciation was a reply to.

links.note: The epic teacher says all who have a body suffer, even gods bowing to higher gods; the quatrain says parting, grievous illness and ruin come together to all who take a body and bids the heart cling to the wise.
links.teaches: The quatrain's advice to cling to the wise is shown to need the epic's wider claim, that no heaven escapes the suffering it names, before it becomes more than comfort.

gains.a: The epic verse gains from the quatrain a remedy, to cling to the wise who see through birth, where the epic only states the diagnosis
gains.b: The quatrain gains the extension to the gods: if even heaven is under suffering, no birth, however high, is a place to rest

links.note: On the sea the merchants are told not to weep over the suffering ripened deeds have brought but to think on the flower-feet of the lord; here the lotus feet of the Lord under the asoka are praised and wished upon the head.
links.teaches: The sea-scene told the crew to take refuge in the feet of the Lord, and this sermon names whose feet they are and why they save.

links.note: The Kural's one who walked on the flower and his noble feet and the epic's wheel-king who walked on the open lotus and his feet which the virtuous praise; both give the lotus walker as the object of devotion.
links.teaches: The epic names what is learned at those feet, five, six and nine, where the couplet names only the reward of long life on earth.

gains.a: The epic verse gains from the couplet the promise attached to reaching the feet, long life on the earth, where it states only knowledge
gains.b: The couplet gains a lotus-walker with a doctrine, who teaches what is to be known, in place of an unnamed figure

links.note: The epic uses the same compound அறவாழி for the lord of dharma ('wheel of dharma' with வேந்தன், king, set against the Kural's reading of the Lord as a sea of virtue).
links.teaches: The epic's use of ஆழி with a king points to the wheel of dharma rather than the sea as the compound's meaning, which the couplet's other seas set against it leaves open.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's claim that nothing else can carry one across, which makes devotion the necessary way
gains.b: The couplet gains an early reading of அறவாழி as the king's wheel of dharma, tied to a doctrine of five, six and nine, not left abstract

links.note: Vijayai said that, like clouds struck by wind, we are scattered by the force of deeds; the teacher says that Indra himself and a small monkey alike eat what their deeds have made.
links.teaches: The mother's saying of parting by deeds becomes a rule with no exemption, since it covers heaven's king, so no rank of birth can be claimed as a refuge.

links.note: The couplet says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who praise the Lord; the epic says that those who have understood both deeds and the Lord's scripture neither exult nor scorn, because every being eats its fruit.
links.teaches: The epic sets the escape in understanding, in a world where even Indra eats his deeds, while the couplet sets it in devotion, so the two give different accounts of how the deeds stop clinging.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's promise that the deeds can fail to cling, which it does not state
gains.b: The couplet gains an account of the mechanism, understanding the two kinds of deeds, and the equal reach of karma over Indra and a monkey, that devotion alone does not give

links.note: The epic says every being from Indra to a monkey eats the fruit of its own deeds, with release by understanding; the Saiva verse says the Lord stands beyond the two deeds and is the seed of the world.
links.teaches: The two give opposite places to the divine in karma: for the Jain verse no one, however high, stands outside deeds, for the Saiva verse the Lord alone does.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Saiva claim of a Lord beyond the two deeds, a figure its own teaching of universal karma has no place for
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a direct rival: that the highest being is also bound to eat his deeds, and that knowledge, not the Lord's stance, ends them

links.note: The epic says those who eat the wounds of other creatures and honey with worms destroy their inner knowledge and are beasts; the couplet says that if men saw flesh as another creature's wound they would not eat it.
links.teaches: Both call flesh another creature's wound, but the epic adds the charge that eating it destroys the eater's discernment, so the loss is the eater's own.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's single image of flesh as a wound, which makes the grammar of its பிறவற்றின் புண் clear
gains.b: The couplet gains an account of what the eater loses, inner discernment and the name of beast, rather than only what the eaten suffers

links.note: The epic defines sila as giving up what the great condemn, and the couplet says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns.
links.teaches: The two agree that sila is the giving up of what is condemned, but the epic's ascetics keep the plucked hair as discipline (2820) where the couplet makes the mark unnecessary.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's insistence that the test of renunciation is what one gives up, not an outward mark, which tests its own list of marks
gains.b: The couplet gains a Jain case where the mark, plucked hair, is itself an austerity borne with patience, so its dismissal of marks is not complete

links.note: Vijayai urged her son to give and said people never give a handful to the poor; the teacher now gives the reason, that a gift in good soil grows like seed and one in barren soil withers.
links.teaches: The mother's plain call to give is answered by an account of why it matters who receives, so giving is a sowing whose crop depends on the field.

links.note: The epic compares gifts to seed in good and poor soil; the quatrain compares even a small virtuous deed that reaches worthy hands to a banyan seed whose shade makes the sky seem small.
links.teaches: Both make the recipient decide the harvest, but the epic adds the poor-soil case, where the gift is lost, which the quatrain's banyan does not show.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the quatrain's picture of a tiny gift that grows greatly, which gives the good-soil half its scale
gains.b: The quatrain gains the opposite case, seed in barren soil that yields little, which shows what a gift to the unworthy costs

source_issues: 2799-2817 and 2821-2822 are printed in eight half-lines in the source and were joined into four lines; the line splits are the editor's.
2807 line 4 (தொழுதகத் கழிப்பர்), 2809 lines 3-4 (பொற்புகுத் திருப்ப), 2811 line 2 (மணிகமாப் பணிகள்) and 2813 (படை மூன்றும், நூல் மூன்று) look corrupt or too terse to read with certainty.
2808 line 2 (வாம னடிகையிற் றொழுது) is open to three readings: a named Vamana, the Lord, or a dancer.
